extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, scientific method, and history of ideas
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and exposition of Francis Bacon's classification of the Idola (cognitive fallacies) and related methodological guidance (role of induction, negative instances, language pitfalls) intended to show how to detect and remove sources of error from human understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idola tribus (Idols of the Tribe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Idola tribus sunt fundata in ipsa natura humana, atque in ipsa tribu seu gente hominum — fallacies rooted in human nature common to all people; the senses and mind (by their constitution) introduce distortions such that human perception cannot be taken as the measure of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that certain general tendencies of the human mind (e.g., seeing order where none exists, analogical projection from human experience) are universal sources of error. The doctrine of the Idols aims to clear the mind of such false notions so it can receive true ones. Remedying these idols is part of the intellectual purification addressed by the redargutiones; compare impressions among people and against facts of Nature; be aware that absolute objectivity is impossible but approximable by critical comparison and correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idola specus (Idols of the Cave / individual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Idola specus sunt idola hominis individui — individual-specific biases arising from a person's own nature, education, conversation, reading, the authors they admire, and peculiar impressions; each person dwells in a particular 'cave' that refracts and corrupts the light of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect and check one's personal biases by noting sources: temperament, upbringing, favored authors, and preconceptions. Compare one's judgments with others and with diverse empirical instances to expose these private distortions. The text contrasts Bacon's view (individual caves) with Plato's collective cave to emphasize individualized corrective measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idola fori (Idols of the Market-place)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sunt idola tanquam ex contractu et societate humani generis ad invicem, quae idola fori propter hominum commercium et consortium appellamus — errors springing from language and social intercourse: words (tesserae notionum) imposed by common use mislead intellect; definitions and technical explanations often fail to restore truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious with common and scholarly vocabulary: ambiguous, imprecise, or socially entrenched words can impose false concepts. Remedy includes careful analysis of terms, reading Locke on language (book III ch.9-11), and resisting the seduction of confident but ill-defined usage. Do not assume that learned definitions automatically correct the confusion caused by popular or conventional language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idola theatri (Idols of the Theatre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sunt idola, quae immigrarunt in animos hominum ex diversis dogmatibus philosophiarum, ac etiam ex perversis legibus demonstrationum; 'idola theatri' are fallacies arising from accepted philosophical systems, dogmas, and defective methods of demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat philosophical systems and inherited modes of demonstration skeptically: systems may be like plays that construct fictitious worlds. Distinguish errors originating in false philosophies and in flawed demonstration rules. The remedy involves detailed critique (Redargutione Philosophiarum and Redargutione Demonstrationum) and openness to reforming foundational principles and axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roger Bacon's 'offendicula' (early classification of impediments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Roger Bacon listed four 'offendicula' that impede the wise: unworthy authority, custom, vulgar opinion, and concealment of ignorance combined with ostentation of apparent wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this alternate taxonomy as a complementary checklist of social and epistemic impediments: question appeals to authority and custom, be skeptical of popular opinion, and beware of rhetorical concealment of ignorance. The text notes the close correspondence between Roger Bacon's list and Bacon's own Idola, and suggests consulting Roger Bacon's Opus Majus/Opus Tertium for detailed refutations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction as requisite to form and test notions and axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is necessary both to give clearness and precision to our notions and to establish true propositions (axioms) which serve as bases for further reasoning; induction used to 'elicit a notion' also elicits axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forming concepts or purported axioms, employ induction: collect observations, form judgments, and generalize cautiously. Recognize there is no strict separation between using induction to craft notions and to justify axioms—both require assembling and comparing instances. Follow Baconian methodological rules (see notes on Aphorism 14) and ensure notions are tested against multiple judgments and facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of the doctrine of Idols: clear the mind of false notions
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of the Idola (fallacies) is to clear the mind of false notions so it may be open to true ones; the identification (indicatio) of idols is of great use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat study of idols as an active preparatory discipline: label and indicate idols to render them detectable and removable. Use these recognitions as preventive and corrective measures during inquiry (comparable function to sophistic elenchus for dialectic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold method of redargution (cleansing intellect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The purgative part is 'absolvitur: redargutione philosopharum, redargutione demonstrationum, et redargutione rationis humanae nativae' — three refutations (of philosophies, demonstrations, and native human reason) are the means to expurgate the intellect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these three corrective operations: (1) critically refute prevailing philosophies and dogmas, (2) examine and correct methods and laws of demonstration, and (3) expose and correct natural tendencies of human reason. These are iterative tasks across parts of Bacon's program (see Partis Secundae and Distributio Operis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of negative instances and counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: A single negative instance, if it admits of no explanation, is sufficient to upset a theory or to require suspension or modification of the theory; negative instances are often peculiarly valuable in calling attention to counteracting causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively seek and privilege contradictory observations when testing theories. Treat unexplained negative instances as grounds to suspend judgment, revise theory, or accumulate further negative evidence. Examples cited: Galileo overturning the weight-based fallacy; Uranus' irregularities leading to Neptune's discovery. Use negative evidence as a corrective instrument rather than dismissing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to overvalue affirmative instances and to seek deceptive parallels (love of system / false analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectus humanus easily supponit maiorem ordinem et aequalitatem in rebus quam invenit, and tends to attach greater importance to affirmative instances supporting a favored opinion than to negative instances; it constructs parallels and correspondences (sometimes falsely).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against confirmation bias and false analogy: be suspicious when one finds pleasing systematic correspondences and parallels. Prefer methods that require demonstration from remote and heterogeneous instances rather than only from striking, simultaneous impressions. Consult Mill and modern treatments of false analogy and non-observation of instances for examples and classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare impressions and inferences with others and with Nature; continual review and correction
rubrics_metrics.description: By comparing our impressions and inferences with those of other men and, above all, by constantly reviewing and correcting our conceptions by comparison with the facts of Nature, we can detect both individual peculiarities and general tendencies to error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use social and empirical checks: cross-compare observations, invite critique, and repeatedly test conceptions against diverse natural facts. This collective and empirical correction mitigates individual and tribal errors and is a practical guide to approach truth despite human cognitive limitations.
